full_judgment:
27. In contracts for sale of immovable property, the fact that a specific time is fixed for payment or for conveyance does not normally make time of the essence. Failure to pay at a fixed time is not per se sufficient to terminate the seller's duty to convey; and failure to convey on the exact date does not per se discharged the buyer. In such agreements, usually time is not be essence of contract the reason being that the law of equity which governs rights of the parties in cases of specific performance of contracts of sale of immovable property, looks not at the letter but at the substance of the agreement. The intention to treat time as the essence of the contract may be evidenced by circumstances which are sufficiently strong to displace the normal presumption that in a contract for sale of real estate, stipulation as to time is not the essence of the contract. 

 37. The law with regard to Specific Performance of Contract is, so far as this country is concerned, condified in the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and under the explanation appended to section 12 of the said Act, a presumption arises in the case of contract to transfer immovable property that its breach cannot be adequately relived by compensation in money. It is true that this presumption is rebuttable but the onus of rebutting it lies heavily on the person who seeks to avoid specific performance. One of the ways in which he can discharged this onus is by showing that the contract has itself provided an alternative method of performance, namely by payment of money. But this must be of such a nature as to show that the stipulation really is to do one of two things at the election of the party who has to do it, that is, either by performance or by payment of money and not merely by showing that the stipulation is to do one certain thing with a penalty attached to secure the performance of that very thing. In the later case, the person will not be relieved from the specific performance of the thing stipulated to be done where that thing is the transference of immovable property, for, the general rule of equity is that if a thing is agreed upon to be done, though there is a penalty annexed to secure its performance, yet the very thing itself must be done. This is the rule that has now been incorporated in section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and it is on the basis of this section that it has been repeatedly held in cases where there are penal clause like those in the contract before us that such clauses do not debar the party who has not defaulted from enforcing specific performance as they are not in the nature of alternative stipulations.
